images.text:
Vanessa: You are going back to Lesotho?
Amy: Yeah. She had someone back out, so Candice asked me to go over with her. Although we have built a lot of momentum through fundraising, people still need to go over and make sure the money is properly put to use. We've made large strides, yet we haven't even scratched the surface yet.
Vanessa: So you will be a project manager?
Amy: More like an assistant. Despite my knowledge of the situation, Candice still has much more experience.
Peter: So this was the news you were going to tell me?
Amy: Aww! Don't worry, Peter. I'll be gone, but not for very long.
Peter: How long?

Amy: Two weeks.
Peter: Do you have to go?
Amy: Haha. You're adorable. I need to take this. Excuse me.
Peter: That is beyond belief! She can be so selfish sometimes.
Vanessa: What? What are you talking about?
Peter: I mean she could have told me about this earlier. Would that be asking too much? She might let me know when she's going to fly to Africa for a week!
Vanessa: Ok, Peter. You need to calm down. You know she is involved in charitable organizations, yet you're acting bewildered.

Peter: Yeah, but does she have to do this now? Must she fly off to another continent when things between us are just getting good?
Vanessa: Well, maybe you should talk about this.
Peter: She'll just overlook everything I say and do what she wants anyway.
Vanessa: I agree with you that she should have told you first. However, the way you are acting right now gives me pause. I've never seen you this controlling before.
Peter: Yeah. Well, you would take her side.
Vanessa: I'm not willing to discuss this any further. You need to get a hold of yourself and then you guys can talk about it later.

Word Order in Concession/ Contrast Clauses

You use concession or contrast clauses to express an idea that suggests the opposite of the main part of the sentence. They are useful in both writing and speaking since they make your language more dynamic and diverse.
Concession clauses have an initial and final position, in other words, before or after the main clause.

Here are the two structures you can use:

conjunction + subject + verb ... , subject + main verb

Example:

Although we have built a lot of momentum through fundraising, people still need to go over and make sure the money is properly put to use.

or

subject + main verb … conjunction + subject + verb

Example:

People still need to go over and make sure the money is properly put to use although we have built a lot of momentum through fundraising.
You can express contrast with however.
For example: I agree with you that she should have told you first. However, the way you are acting right now gives me pause.

You can also express contrast with the coordinating conjunction yet.
For example:
You know she is involved in charitable organizations, yet you are acting bewildered.
